title: Jeremiah 13:1–11
context: Jeremiah 13:1–11 is told by Jeremiah in the first person. The LORD tells him to buy a linen belt, wear it, and keep it out of water (13:1–2), then to hide it in a cleft of the rock by the Euphrates (13:4–5); after many days he digs it up and finds it ruined (13:6–7). The LORD then explains the sign: so he will ruin the pride of Judah and Jerusalem (13:9), a people who refuse to hear and go after other gods (13:10). As a belt clings to the waist, so he caused Israel and Judah to cling to him, “that they may be to me for a people, for a name, for praise, and for glory; but they would not hear.” (13:11; compare Deuteronomy 10:20; 26:19). Readers differ on how the sign took place. Some take it as an enacted sign involving real journeys; others think the journeys were seen in a vision or told as a parable, partly because the Euphrates was several hundred miles away and the account implies two round trips. The Hebrew name that the WEB renders as the Euphrates is usually that river’s name, but some suggest a nearer place with a similar name, such as Parah near Anathoth (compare Joshua 18:23), possibly chosen to evoke the Euphrates and the threat from that direction. These notes name both readings without deciding between them. Both traditions read the meaning of the sign as shared ground: the LORD bound his people to himself for his praise and glory, and their refusal to listen leaves them ruined like the belt.

verses.text: The LORD said to me, “Go, and buy yourself a linen belt, and put it on your waist, and don’t put it in water.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah, “Go, and buy yourself a linen belt, and put it on your waist, and don’t put it in water.” Arminian readers note that linen was associated with priestly garments, though how far that association is intended here is uncertain, and they see the belt as a picture of Israel’s close relationship with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the priestly association loosely. They note that the instruction not to put the belt in water may stress that it was new and clean when first worn, and they read the action as the beginning of a sign the LORD will explain later in the passage.

verses.text: So I bought a belt according to the LORD’s word, and put it on my waist.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says, “So I bought a belt according to the LORD’s word, and put it on my waist.” Arminian readers note the prophet’s simple obedience before he understands the meaning of the sign, and they see in it an example of trusting God’s word even when its purpose is not yet clear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same obedience and observe that the prophet’s own body becomes part of the message. They read the verse as part of a pattern in which prophets act out God’s word, though readers differ on whether this sign was performed physically or seen in a vision.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me the second time, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word came to Jeremiah the second time. Arminian readers note that the sign unfolds in stages, with the LORD giving fresh instructions at each step, and they see the prophet waiting for God’s word rather than acting on his own initiative or interpretation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the repeated coming of the LORD’s word stresses that the whole sign is directed by God. They observe that the prophet does not invent the symbolism but receives it, and they read the verse as underlining divine initiative in the prophetic ministry.

verses.text: “Take the belt that you have bought, which is on your waist, and arise, go to the Euphrates, and hide it there in a cleft of the rock.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah to take the belt and go to the Euphrates and hide it in a cleft of the rock. Arminian readers note that the name is usually the river’s name, which may point to Babylon and Assyria, while some suggest a nearer place such as Parah (compare Joshua 18:23); they hold both readings open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note both readings of the place name and the question whether the journey was physical or visionary. They observe that on either reading the location evokes the direction from which judgment and exile would come, and they do not settle the geography.

verses.text: So I went and hid it by the Euphrates, as the LORD commanded me.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says, “So I went and hid it by the Euphrates, as the LORD commanded me.” Arminian readers note that the prophet’s obedience is again stressed, and they observe that if the Euphrates is meant literally, the journey would have been long and demanding, though readers differ on this.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repeated phrase as the LORD commanded me, which emphasizes exact obedience. They hold open whether the journey was an actual trip, a vision, or a parable told in narrative form, and they read the verse as part of a sign whose meaning matters more than its mechanics.

verses.text: After many days, the LORD said to me, “Arise, go to the Euphrates, and take the belt from there, which I commanded you to hide there.”
verses.arminianNotes: After many days, the LORD tells Jeremiah to go back to the Euphrates and take the belt from where he hid it. Arminian readers note that the passage of many days allows time for the belt to decay, and they see the delay as part of the sign’s picture of a long process of corruption.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same delay and read it as part of God’s careful design of the sign. They observe that the second journey adds to the difficulty if the trips were literal, which is one reason some readers favor a vision or a nearer location, without deciding the matter.

verses.text: Then I went to the Euphrates, and dug, and took the belt from the place where I had hidden it; and behold, the belt was ruined. It was profitable for nothing.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah finds the belt ruined: “It was profitable for nothing.” Arminian readers note the striking picture of something once close and useful now spoiled, and they see it as a warning that a people who turn from God lose the very purpose for which they were chosen and made.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same image and read the ruined belt as a picture of what Judah has become through idolatry and pride. They observe that the phrase profitable for nothing returns in 13:10, linking the object directly to the people it represents.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Then the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah, saying what the sign means. Arminian readers note that the sign is not left without explanation, and they see the LORD’s care to make his message clear to his prophet and, through him, to the people who need to hear it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the interpretation, like the instructions, comes from the LORD. They observe that prophetic signs in Scripture are typically explained by God’s word, and they read the verse as the turning point from action to meaning in the passage.

verses.text: “The LORD says, ‘In this way I will ruin the pride of Judah, and the great pride of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “In this way I will ruin the pride of Judah, and the great pride of Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note that pride is singled out as the root problem, and they see God’s judgment as aimed at humbling a people who have trusted in themselves rather than in him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same focus on pride and read the ruin as God’s just response to a people who have exalted themselves. Both traditions see pride as a central sin in the prophets and read the verse as a warning that God opposes the proud.

verses.text: This evil people, who refuse to hear my words, who walk in the stubbornness of their heart, and have gone after other gods to serve them and to worship them, will even be as this belt, which is profitable for nothing.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD calls Judah an evil people who refuse to hear his words, walk in the stubbornness of their heart, and go after other gods. Arminian readers note that the refusal is described as their own choice and habit, and they see the comparison with the ruined belt as the result of persistent rejection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase the stubbornness of their heart, which recurs in Jeremiah, and they read it as a description of a heart turned from God. They observe that both traditions see in the verse a link between refusing God’s word, idolatry, and becoming profitable for nothing.

verses.text: For as the belt clings to the waist of a man, so I have caused the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah to cling to me,’ says the LORD; ‘that they may be to me for a people, for a name, for praise, and for glory; but they would not hear.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that as a belt clings to a man’s waist, so he caused Israel and Judah to cling to him, “that they may be to me for a people, for a name, for praise, and for glory; but they would not hear.” Arminian readers note the closeness of the bond and the tragedy of refusal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the echo of Deuteronomy 10:20, “You shall cling to him”, and of Deuteronomy 26:19, named without harmonizing. They read the verse as stating God’s purpose in choosing his people, for his praise and glory, and the grief of their refusal to hear.
